title: The optimisation of agri / ecotourism strenghts and opportunities and negation of threats and weaknesses

lessons.title: Agritourism and ecotourism on South African farms
lessons.html:
Adding a tourism enterprise

Agritourism brings visitors to a working farm: farm stays, pick-your-own fruit, wine and olive tastings, farm stalls, 4x4 and hiking trails, school visits, weddings and festivals. Ecotourism focuses on nature: game viewing, birding, wildflowers, conservancies and community-based experiences. South Africa's scenery, wildlife, cultural diversity and farming heritage give many farms real tourism potential, and tourism can smooth out the seasonal and drought-related swings of farm income.

Why a SWOT analysis

Before investing, analyse the venture with a SWOT:

  • Strengths (internal): what the farm already has, such as scenery, a historic farmhouse, a river, game, a well-known product, skilled hosts.
  • Weaknesses (internal): poor road access, limited capital, no hospitality skills, water shortages, farm operations that clash with visitors.
  • Opportunities (external): growing domestic tourism, nearby tourist routes (e.g. wine routes, the Garden Route, Panorama Route), weak rand attracting foreign visitors, demand for authentic rural experiences.
  • Threats (external): crime perception, economic downturns, competition, drought, disease outbreaks, load-shedding, changing travel trends.

Doing the analysis properly

Involve the family, staff and, where relevant, the local community. Use facts: visitor numbers in the area, competitor prices and occupancy, distance from cities and airports. A frank list of weaknesses is more useful than an optimistic brochure. Rank each item by importance so you can focus on what matters most.

lessons.title: Optimising strengths and opportunities
lessons.html:
Turning the SWOT into strategy

The SWOT is only useful if it leads to action. A common approach matches internal and external factors:

OpportunitiesThreats
StrengthsSO: use strengths to grab opportunitiesST: use strengths to reduce threats
WeaknessesWO: fix weaknesses by using opportunitiesWT: minimise weaknesses and avoid threats

Optimising strengths and opportunities (SO)

  • A citrus farm on a scenic route can offer orchard tours and a farm stall selling juice and marmalade, linking production to tourism.
  • A Karoo sheep farm with dark skies can offer stargazing and lamb-themed dining.
  • Game on a Limpopo cattle-and-game farm can support guided drives and birding weekends.

Developing a unique selling point

Visitors choose experiences that feel authentic. Tell the story of the farm and its people, use local food and crafts, and offer hands-on activities such as milking demonstrations or harvest days. Partner with local communities for guiding, crafts and cultural experiences, which spreads benefits and strengthens the product.

Marketing

Use online booking platforms, social media, tourism route associations and provincial tourism bodies. Collect reviews and respond to them. Price according to the market and your costs, not guesswork. Grading by the Tourism Grading Council of South Africa can build trust for accommodation.

Integrating with farming

Plan visitor areas so they do not disrupt operations or biosecurity. Keep visitors away from spraying, machinery and animal handling, and schedule activities around the farm calendar.

lessons.title: Negating weaknesses and threats
lessons.html:
Reducing risk

Addressing weaknesses

  • Skills: train staff in hospitality, guiding and first aid, or partner with experienced operators.
  • Capital: start small (a farm stall or self-catering cottage) and grow from income; investigate tourism development funds and partnerships.
  • Access and signage: maintain roads to visitor areas and provide clear directions.
  • Water and power: invest in rainwater harvesting, solar power and backup systems; tourism increases demand.

Managing threats

  • Safety and security: controlled access, good lighting, emergency contacts, staff trained to respond. Visitors are owed a safe environment; dangerous animals, dams and machinery must be fenced off or clearly signposted.
  • Legal compliance: obtain zoning or land-use approval where required, liquor and food licences, health certificates and public liability insurance. Employees in the tourism enterprise fall under the OHS Act 85 of 1993 and labour laws like any farm worker.
  • Biosecurity: visitors can carry disease. Use footbaths, restrict access to animal houses, and follow movement controls during outbreaks.
  • Market shocks: diversify markets (domestic and international, schools, corporate groups) and keep the core farm profitable so tourism remains a supplement, not a lifeline.
  • Environmental damage: limit vehicle tracks, manage waste and sewage, and keep visitor numbers within what the land can carry.

Monitoring

Track occupancy, income per visitor, costs, reviews and incidents. Review the SWOT every year because markets and risks change.

Key points

  • A SWOT separates internal strengths and weaknesses from external opportunities and threats.
  • Use strengths to capture opportunities and build a unique, authentic experience.
  • Fix weaknesses step by step and start small.
  • Manage safety, legal compliance, biosecurity and environmental impacts.
  • Review the SWOT and results annually.
